claims.source: Other unconventional T cells are known to behave similarly such as CD1d-restricted NKT cells, which can acquire a Tfh phenotype and provide B cell help through both cognate and non-cognate interactions (Clerici et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claims.claim: IgG antibodies against MA and glycolipid lipoarabinomannan exist in TB patients.
claims.source: Additional work will look at whether DN1 or other group 1 CD1-restricted T cells can functionally act as Tfh cells to provide B cell help, as may be suggested by the existence of IgG antibodies against MA and glycolipid lipoarabinomannan in TB patients (Correia-Neves et al., 2019; Schleicher et al., 2002; Pan et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: The persistence of protein antigen has been shown to improve the quality of protective immunity.
claims.source: While the persistence of protein antigen has been shown to improve the quality of protective immunity (Demento et al., 2012; Tamburini et al., 2014; Bioley et al., 2015; Silva et al., 2013), it is not yet known how lipid antigen persistence may affect the protective efficacy of lipid-specific T cells.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: It is not yet known how lipid antigen persistence may affect the protective efficacy of lipid-specific T cells.
claims.source: While the persistence of protein antigen has been shown to improve the quality of protective immunity (Demento et al., 2012; Tamburini et al., 2014; Bioley et al., 2015; Silva et al., 2013), it is not yet known how lipid antigen persistence may affect the protective efficacy of lipid-specific T cells.
claims.evidence: This is an acknowledgment of gaps in current knowledge.

claims.claim: Antigen persistence increases the probability of T cell/DC encounters by increasing the time that the antigen is available.
claims.source: At the very least, antigen persistence increases the probability of T cell/DC encounters by increasing the time that the antigen is available.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the potential benefits of antigen persistence.

results.result: BCN and MA-BCN nanoparticles were successfully fabricated with consistent size (~360 nm), monodisperse distribution (PDI ~0.2), and preserved cubic internal architecture. MA encapsulation did not disturb BCN structure, and BCN showed superior MA encapsulation efficiency compared to PLGA nanoparticles.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C67 provide converging evidence from DLS, cryo-TEM, TEM, and SAXS demonstrating successful BCN fabrication with preserved structure after MA loading. Claim C69 shows superior encapsulation efficiency of BCN versus PLGA. The characterization is comprehensive with multiple orthogonal techniques supporting the structural claims.

results.result: BCN retain cargo within the endolysosomal compartment more effectively than PLGA nanoparticles, with Texas Red-Dextran loaded BCN remaining primarily in lysosomes while PLGA-NP cargo distributed to both lysosomes and cytosol.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C71 are supported by confocal microscopy data (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) showing differential intracellular localization. The Pearson correlation analysis provides quantitative support for the qualitative observation of enhanced lysosomal retention by BCN.

results.result: In vitro, both MA-BCN and MA-PLGA effectively activated MA-specific T cells, with MA-BCN showing superior activation compared to free MA. However, blank PLGA-NP exhibited considerable background stimulation, particularly for human M11 T cells, while blank BCN showed minimal background immunostimulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C78 are well-supported by in vitro T cell activation data (Figures 2A-D) showing dose-dependent responses. The differential background stimulation between blank BCN and PLGA-NP is clearly demonstrated, though the mechanism underlying PLGA's background effect is not explained. The comparison is rigorous with appropriate controls.

results.result: In vivo, MA-BCN induced significantly higher DN1 T cell proliferation and activation than MA-PLGA in draining lymph nodes and lungs at 1 week post-vaccination, with MA-PLGA showing no significant difference from blank PLGA.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C80 are supported by in vivo data (Figures 2E-G) showing superior performance of MA-BCN despite MA-PLGA's better in vitro performance at lower concentrations. This apparent contradiction is addressed by the authors' discussion of PLGA fragility and antigen loss in vivo. Statistical significance is clearly demonstrated.

results.result: MA-BCN vaccination resulted in MA-specific DN1 T cell activation and proliferation at 6 weeks post-vaccination, with no activation of Ag85B-specific p25 T cells, demonstrating antigen-specific long-term T cell responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C82 are supported by data in Figures 3B-D showing significant DN1 but not p25 T cell responses at 6 weeks. The antigen specificity is well-controlled using two different TCR transgenic T cell populations. This establishes the key finding of MA persistence.

results.result: Dual-loaded Ag85B-MA-BCN nanoparticles (380 nm, 70% protein encapsulation efficiency) activated both p25 and DN1 T cells at 1 week post-vaccination, but only DN1 T cells remained activated at 6 weeks, demonstrating differential persistence of lipid versus protein antigens.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C87 are supported by characterization data (Figure 4A) and in vivo T cell activation data (Figures 4B-H). The differential persistence between MA and Ag85B is clearly demonstrated at the 6-week timepoint. This is a key finding showing antigen-specific differences in persistence within the same nanocarrier.

results.result: BCN encapsulation is required for MA persistence, as demonstrated by comparing MA-BCN versus free MA pulsed dendritic cells, where only MA-BCN maintained T cell activation at 6 weeks post-vaccination.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C89 are supported by data in Figures 5B-C showing equivalent short-term responses but only MA-BCN maintaining responses at 6 weeks. The experimental design appropriately controls for differential T cell activation capacity by adjusting MA concentrations. This establishes the requirement for nanocarrier encapsulation.

results.result: The structure of the encapsulating nanoparticle (BCN versus MC) did not significantly affect MA antigen persistence, as both MA-BCN and MA-MC showed similar ability to activate DN1 T cells at both short-term and long-term timepoints.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C91 are supported by data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B-C comparing BCN and MC formulations. The conclusion that nanoparticle structure is not critical for persistence is reasonable, though only two structures were tested. Additional nanocarrier types would strengthen this conclusion.

results.result: MA persistence is not unique to intratracheal vaccination, as DN1 T cell activation was detected at 6 weeks post-vaccination through both intravenous and subcutaneous routes.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C93 are supported by data in Figures 5D-F showing DN1 T cell responses at 6 weeks via multiple vaccination routes. This demonstrates the robustness of MA persistence across different administration methods, though the cellular location of persistence may differ by route (as authors acknowledge in C163-C165).

results.result: Vaccination with attenuated Mtb reproduced MA persistence without bacterial burden at 6 weeks, with DN1 but not p25 T cell activation, demonstrating that MA persistence occurs with live attenuated vaccine and can be mimicked by nanocarrier formulations.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C97 are supported by bacterial burden data (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A) and T cell activation data (Figures 5D-F, Figure 5—figure supplement 2B-D). This is a critical control showing that the nanocarrier system recapitulates a phenomenon observed with attenuated bacteria, strengthening the biological relevance of the findings.

results.result: DiD-labeled BCN remained localized almost exclusively in the lung for up to 6 weeks post-intratracheal administration, with fluorescence detectable at 6 weeks suggesting intact BCN structure. DiD-BCN was primarily found in alveolar macrophages at both early and late timepoints.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C102 are supported by IVIS imaging (Figure 6A) and flow cytometry (Figure 6C). The inference about intact BCN structure (C100) is reasonable given DiD's rapid quenching in aqueous environments, though direct structural analysis would be more definitive. The biodistribution data clearly establishes lung localization and AM uptake.

results.result: Alveolar macrophages are the primary cellular location of MA persistence after intratracheal vaccination, but cannot directly present MA to DN1 T cells due to lack of CD1b expression. MA presentation requires transfer to CD1b-expressing dendritic cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C110 are supported by enrichment experiments (Figure 6E) and prior literature on CD1b expression (C108). The requirement for DCs is clearly demonstrated by the lack of T cell activation when AMs are cultured with T cells alone. The mechanism of MA transfer from AMs to DCs remains speculative (C107) but is a reasonable inference.

results.result: MA-BCN vaccination induced memory DN1 T cells (CD44+CD62L+) that persisted for 40 days in blood. RNA-seq analysis identified 995 differentially expressed genes, with memory DN1 T cells clustering most closely to Tfh cells by principal component analysis.
results.evaluation: Claims C111-C116 are supported by flow cytometry (Figure 7B-C) and RNA-seq data (Figure 7D-E). The PCA analysis clearly shows memory DN1 T cells clustering with Tfh, Treg, and Texh populations, and most closely with Tfh when this subset is isolated. The experimental design using bone marrow chimeras is appropriate for long-term studies.

results.result: Memory DN1 T cells exhibited a Tfh-like phenotype with upregulation of key Tfh markers (BCL6, TCF7, CXCR5, CXCR4, ICOS, SAP, PD-1, TIGIT, CTLA4, EOMES) and downregulation of Tfh inhibitors (KLF2, CCR7, IL-7R). Flow cytometry confirmed increased CXCR5+PD-1+ cells and proliferation (KI67+) in memory but not naïve DN1 T cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C117-C126 are supported by RNA-seq data (Figure 7F) and flow cytometry validation (Figures 7G-J). The convergence of transcriptomic and protein-level data strongly supports the Tfh-like phenotype. The gene enrichment analysis showing mitotic cell cycle processes (Figure 7I) aligns with the KI67 data. This is a comprehensive characterization of the memory phenotype.

results.result: The BCN platform enables dual encapsulation and simultaneous in vivo activation of both lipid (MA) and protein (Ag85B) antigen-specific T cells, representing the first demonstration of a dual protein and lipid loaded nanocarrier effectively stimulating both T cell populations simultaneously in vivo.
results.evaluation: Claims C10, C15, C58, C60 are supported by experimental data showing activation of both DN1 and p25 T cells with Ag85B-MA-BCN (Figures 4B-D). The novelty claim (C130) cannot be independently verified but is reasonable given the limited literature on lipid antigen vaccines. The dual-loading capability is a significant technical achievement enabling multicomponent vaccine strategies.

results.result: Only MA, but not Ag85B, persisted within alveolar macrophages after vaccination with dual-loaded MA-Ag85B-BCN, suggesting lipid antigen persistence may be a unique characteristic of subunit vaccines containing lipid antigens.
results.evaluation: Claims C11, C61 are directly supported by the differential T cell responses at 6 weeks (Figures 4E-H). The inference about unique characteristics of lipid antigens (C62) is reasonable but requires additional lipid antigens to be tested for generalizability. The differential persistence is a key finding distinguishing lipid from protein antigen behavior.

results.result: MA persistence for 6 weeks post-vaccination is a robust phenomenon that occurs independently of the encapsulating vector (BCN, MC, or attenuated Mtb) and vaccination route (IT, IV, SC), but requires some form of encapsulation as DC internalization alone was insufficient.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C57, C166-C168 are supported by data across multiple figures (Figures 3, 5) showing persistence across different conditions. The requirement for encapsulation is demonstrated by the free MA versus MA-BCN pulsed DC comparison. This establishes MA persistence as a general phenomenon rather than an artifact of specific formulation or delivery conditions.

results.result: Despite differentiating in an environment of persistent antigen exposure, memory DN1 T cells exhibited a gene expression profile similar to Tfh cells rather than exhausted T cells, with upregulation of TCF7 and BCL6 that sustain a non-exhausted phenotype.
results.evaluation: Claims C170-C172 are supported by RNA-seq data (Figure 7) and literature on T cell exhaustion. The finding that persistent antigen does not lead to exhaustion is important and aligns with prior work on antigen archiving (C172). The inflammatory context rather than mere antigen persistence appears critical for determining T cell fate.

results.result: MA-BCN demonstrated superior in vivo stimulatory capacity compared to MA-PLGA despite PLGA's better in vitro performance. Blank PLGA-NP showed considerable background stimulation while blank BCN showed minimal immunostimulation, making PEG-b-PPS a promising polymer for subunit vaccine formulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C54, C76-C78, C135 are supported by direct comparison data (Figure 2). The explanation for the in vitro/in vivo discrepancy (C133) is reasonable and supported by citation. However, the conclusion about PLGA's limited effectiveness for lipid antigen delivery (C134) is based on a single formulation and may not generalize to all PLGA formulations. The low background of BCN is a significant advantage.

results.result: The lack of Ag85B persistence may be due to protein leakage from BCN aqueous pores, while MA's extreme hydrophobicity may contribute to its prolonged persistence. Peptide antigens could potentially be modified with hydrophobic tails for enhanced retention.
results.evaluation: Claims C157 and C159 are reasonable inferences supported by prior observations (citations) and chemical properties of MA, but lack direct experimental evidence in this study. Claim C158 is speculation about future modifications. While the hypotheses are plausible, they require experimental validation such as direct measurement of antigen release kinetics or testing of lipidated peptides.

results.result: Persistent lipid depots from BCN vaccination could offer long-lasting immune responses by increasing T cell/DC encounter probability, though the effect of lipid antigen persistence on protective efficacy remains unknown.
results.evaluation: Claim C16 is speculative about long-lasting immune responses without protection data. Claims C148 and C182 cite prior work on protein antigen persistence improving immunity, but C183 acknowledges that effects of lipid antigen persistence are unknown. Claim C184 is a reasonable inference but the study lacks functional protection experiments. Future work is explicitly needed to assess protective capacity.

results.result: While MA persists within alveolar macrophages after pulmonary vaccination, the exact cellular localization after SC, IV, or attenuated Mtb vaccination remains to be determined, with other macrophage types potentially involved.
results.evaluation: Claims C163-C165 appropriately acknowledge limitations of the current study. The inference that AM localization is route-dependent (C163) is reasonable given anatomical considerations (C164). This represents an honest assessment of what the data do and do not show, identifying clear directions for future work.

results.result: The authors characterized BCN and PLGA nanoparticles loaded with mycolic acid (MA), demonstrating that MA-BCN maintained the characteristic cubic internal organization without disruption, had consistent size (~364 nm) and monodispersity, and showed superior MA encapsulation efficiency compared to PLGA nanoparticles.
results.evaluation: All three reviewers acknowledged the characterization studies without raising concerns. The first reviewer stated 'the authors generate mycolic acid (MA)-loaded BCN and perform a series of characterization studies to demonstrate the superior performance of this new formulation.' The second reviewer confirmed 'they were able to load the lipid, mycolic acid, into their nanoparticles without disrupting the architecture.' No methodological concerns were raised about these characterization data.

results.result: In vitro T cell activation assays showed that both MA-BCN and MA-PLGA effectively activated MA-specific T cells and induced IFN-γ production, with MA-BCN significantly better than free MA. However, blank PLGA-NP showed considerable background stimulation, while blank BCN showed minimal background immunostimulation.
results.evaluation: The second reviewer explicitly noted that 'the loaded particles activated T cells both in vitro and in vivo' without raising concerns about the in vitro data. The first reviewer described the data as 'convincing.' The differential performance between BCN and PLGA platforms, including the background stimulation findings, was not questioned by any reviewer.

results.result: In vivo vaccination with MA-BCN induced significantly higher DN1 T cell proliferation and activation in draining lymph nodes and lungs at 1 week post-vaccination compared to MA-PLGA, which showed no significant difference from blank PLGA controls.
results.evaluation: The second reviewer confirmed the in vivo activation findings, stating 'the loaded particles activated T cells both in vitro and in vivo.' The first reviewer noted the 'superior performance of this new formulation relative to the original one' and called the data 'convincing.' The comparison between BCN and PLGA platforms was accepted without methodological critique.

results.result: Pulmonary administration of MA-BCN elicited MA-specific T cell responses that persisted for 6 weeks post-vaccination, with significant DN1 T cell activation and proliferation detected in lymph nodes, lung, and spleen, while no activation of Ag85B-specific T cells was observed.
results.evaluation: The second reviewer explicitly acknowledged this finding: 'mycolic acid-specific T cells were able to be activated 6 weeks post-vaccination.' The first reviewer highlighted 'antigen persistence, a quality needed to sustain responses after vaccination' as a key finding. All reviewers accepted these long-term activation data without expressing concerns about the methodology or interpretation.

results.result: Dual encapsulation of MA and Ag85B within BCN (Ag85B-MA-BCN) activated both MA- and Ag85B-specific T cells at 1 week post-vaccination, but at 6 weeks only MA-specific DN1 T cells remained activated while Ag85B-specific p25 T cells showed no increased activation compared to controls.
results.evaluation: The second reviewer noted this differential persistence: 'when they vaccinated with particles loaded with both lipid and protein antigens, they found that the lipid antigen persisted, and mycolic acid-specific T cells were able to be activated 6 weeks post-vaccination, in contrast to peptide-specific T cells.' The first reviewer acknowledged the dual incorporation capability. No concerns were raised about these findings.

results.result: MA persistence required nanocarrier encapsulation, as DN1 T cell responses at 6 weeks were only detected with MA-BCN vaccination but not with free MA-pulsed dendritic cells, demonstrating that BCN encapsulation contributed to MA persistence.
results.evaluation: The second reviewer explicitly stated 'persistence required the nanoparticle encapsulation, rather than free lipid.' The first reviewer noted this as part of the demonstration of 'superior performance' and 'antigen persistence.' The experimental design comparing encapsulated versus free antigen was accepted without methodological concerns.

results.result: MA persistence was independent of vaccination route, as DN1 T cell activation was detected at 6 weeks post-vaccination through intravenous, subcutaneous, and intratracheal routes, as well as with attenuated Mtb vaccination.
results.evaluation: The second reviewer confirmed 'it was independent of route (intratracheal, intravenous, or subcutaneous) of administration.' The third reviewer noted 'Authors assay different routes of vaccination' without raising concerns about the findings. The demonstration of route-independence was accepted as valid by all reviewers.

results.result: Biodistribution studies using DiD-labeled BCN showed that MA-BCN persisted primarily within alveolar macrophages in the lung for up to 6 weeks post-vaccination, with enriched alveolar macrophages from vaccinated mice inducing significantly higher DN1 T cell activation than flow-through fractions when co-cultured with dendritic cells.
results.evaluation: The second reviewer explicitly described this finding: 'the nanoparticle encapsulated lipid antigen was primarily stored in lung alveolar macrophages and that CD1b+ dendritic cells presented the antigen to mycolic acid specific T cells.' The first reviewer accepted the mechanistic studies without concern. The biodistribution and cellular localization data were not questioned by any reviewer.

results.result: Alveolar macrophages could not directly present MA to DN1 T cells in the absence of dendritic cells, suggesting that MA is transferred from alveolar macrophages to CD1b-expressing dendritic cells for presentation, as CD1b is not expressed on alveolar macrophages.
results.evaluation: The second reviewer confirmed this mechanism: 'CD1b+ dendritic cells presented the antigen to mycolic acid specific T cells.' The requirement for dendritic cells in the presentation mechanism was accepted without challenge. No reviewer questioned the interpretation that antigen transfer occurs from macrophages to dendritic cells.

results.result: MA-specific T cells in MA-BCN-vaccinated mice differentiated into a proliferating T follicular helper (Tfh)-like phenotype, as demonstrated by RNA-seq showing upregulation of Tfh markers (BCL6, TCF7, CXCR5, CXCR4, ICOS, SAP) and flow cytometry confirming increased CXCR5+PD-1+ cells and Ki67+ proliferating cells, with memory DN1 T cells clustering most closely to Tfh cells by principal component analysis.
results.evaluation: The second reviewer explicitly acknowledged this finding: 'the memory T cell population phenotypically resembled T follicular helper, regulatory T cells, and exhausted T cells. Interestingly, while a large percentage of these lipid antigen specific T cells in the lymph nodes, lung and spleen were CXCR5+PD1+, the cells were still proliferating (Ki67+).' The first reviewer called the study 'comprehensive' and the data 'convincing.' The transcriptomic and phenotypic characterization was accepted without methodological concerns.

results.result: The BCN platform allows for dual encapsulation and in vivo activation of both lipid and protein antigen-specific T cells, representing the first demonstration of a dual protein and lipid loaded nanocarrier effectively stimulating both types of antigen-specific T cells simultaneously in vivo.
results.evaluation: The first reviewer highlighted this as a key contribution: 'allowing for the dual incorporation of lipid and protein antigens' and noted it 'provides important new insights relevant to the TB vaccine field.' The third reviewer emphasized the novelty: 'This work is novel, and it brings new data of high relevance for the TB vaccine field pointing to alternative formulations and antigens.' The claim of being first was not challenged.

results.result: BCN leads to persistent lipid depots that could offer long-lasting immune responses, with lipid antigen persistence being a potentially unique characteristic of subunit vaccines containing lipid antigens that occurs robustly and independently of vector and vaccination route.
results.evaluation: While the first reviewer noted 'antigen persistence, a quality needed to sustain responses after vaccination,' the claim that this 'could offer long-lasting immune responses' is speculative. The third reviewer noted 'no protection studies are provided,' indicating that the functional benefit of persistence remains undemonstrated. The persistence phenomenon itself is supported, but its impact on protective immunity is uncertain.

results.result: The incorporation of lipid antigens into subunit vaccine strategies has been underexplored, the characteristics of vaccine-induced lipid-specific memory T cells have remained elusive, and research on subunit vaccines containing lipid antigens is limited.
results.evaluation: The third reviewer explicitly confirmed this gap: 'Most subunit vaccines integrate protein antigens formulated with adjuvants and there are few examples of the performance of subunit vaccines integrating lipid antigens.' The first reviewer acknowledged this addresses an important need by noting the work 'suggests that alternative antigens to proteins could be used in TB vaccine formulations.' The characterization of this gap was not challenged.

comparisons.comparison: Both evaluations support the BCN characterization claims (C63-C69). OpenEval emphasizes the comprehensive multi-technique approach and superior encapsulation efficiency. Peer reviewers acknowledged the characterization studies without methodological concerns, with one noting the ability to load lipid without disrupting architecture.

Perfect agreement on in vitro T cell activation data (C72-C78). Both evaluations support the dose-dependent responses and differential background stimulation between BCN and PLGA. OpenEval notes the mechanism underlying PLGA's background effect is unexplained, while peer reviewers found the data 'convincing' without raising concerns.

Both support the in vivo superiority of MA-BCN over MA-PLGA (C79-C80, C54). OpenEval addresses the apparent in vitro/in vivo contradiction through discussion of PLGA fragility. Peer reviewers accepted the 'superior performance' and 'convincing' data without questioning the discrepancy.

Both evaluations support the 6-week persistence of MA-specific T cell responses (C81-C82, C56). OpenEval emphasizes the antigen-specific controls using two TCR transgenic populations. Peer reviewers explicitly acknowledged the 6-week activation finding as a key demonstration of antigen persistence.

Both support the differential persistence between MA and Ag85B antigens (C85-C87, C10, C58, C60-C61). OpenEval highlights this as showing antigen-specific differences within the same nanocarrier. Peer reviewers confirmed the differential persistence and accepted the dual incorporation capability without concerns.

Both evaluations support the requirement for nanocarrier encapsulation for persistence (C88-C89, C57). OpenEval notes the appropriate experimental design controlling for differential activation capacity. Peer reviewers explicitly stated 'persistence required the nanoparticle encapsulation, rather than free lipid.'

Both support the route-independence of MA persistence (C92-C93, C12-C13, C95). OpenEval demonstrates robustness across administration methods while acknowledging potential differences in cellular location. Peer reviewers confirmed independence of route without raising concerns about the findings.

Both support the biodistribution and cellular localization findings (C98-C104, C110). OpenEval notes the inference about intact BCN structure is reasonable but direct analysis would be more definitive. Peer reviewers explicitly described the storage in alveolar macrophages and DC presentation without questioning the methodology.

Both evaluations support the DC requirement for antigen presentation (C103-C110). OpenEval notes the mechanism of MA transfer from AMs to DCs is speculative but reasonable. Peer reviewers confirmed the CD1b+ DC presentation mechanism without challenging the interpretation.

Both support the Tfh-like memory phenotype characterization (C111-C116). OpenEval emphasizes the PCA clustering analysis and appropriate bone marrow chimera design. Peer reviewers acknowledged the phenotypic resemblance to Tfh, Treg, and exhausted T cells, noting the proliferative capacity despite CXCR5+PD1+ expression.

Both support the comprehensive transcriptomic and protein-level characterization of the Tfh-like phenotype (C117-C126). OpenEval highlights the convergence of RNA-seq and flow cytometry data. Peer reviewers called the study 'comprehensive' and data 'convincing' without methodological concerns.

Both support the dual-loading capability and novelty claims (C10, C15, C58, C60, C130-C131). OpenEval notes the novelty claim cannot be independently verified but is reasonable. Peer reviewers highlighted this as a key contribution providing 'important new insights' and bringing 'new data of high relevance' without challenging the first-in-field claim.

Both support the differential persistence between MA and Ag85B (C11, C61-C62). OpenEval notes the inference about unique lipid antigen characteristics requires testing additional lipids for generalizability. Peer reviewers accepted the differential persistence finding without expressing concerns about generalizability.

Both evaluations rate claims about long-lasting immune responses as UNCERTAIN (C16, C62, C168). OpenEval notes speculation about protective capacity without protection data. Peer reviewers acknowledged persistence as 'a quality needed to sustain responses' but noted 'no protection studies are provided,' indicating functional benefit remains undemonstrated.

OpenEval supports the differential intracellular localization findings from confocal microscopy (C70-C71) with quantitative Pearson correlation analysis. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses these localization claims.

OpenEval supports the comparison between BCN and MC formulations (C90-C91), concluding nanoparticle structure is not critical for persistence, though notes only two structures were tested. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses this structural comparison.

OpenEval supports the comparison with attenuated bacteria showing the nanocarrier system recapitulates natural infection phenomena (C94-C97). This critical control strengthens biological relevance but was not specifically addressed in peer review evaluations.

OpenEval supports MA persistence as a general phenomenon across conditions (C56-C57, C166-C168), with encapsulation requirement demonstrated. While peer reviewers accepted individual persistence findings, no specific evaluation addresses the generalizability claim across multiple conditions.

OpenEval supports the finding that persistent antigen does not lead to exhaustion (C170-C172), noting inflammatory context rather than antigen persistence determines T cell fate. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses the exhaustion question.

OpenEval supports BCN's superior performance and low background (C54, C76-C78, C133-C136) but notes the conclusion about PLGA's limited effectiveness may not generalize to all PLGA formulations. While peer reviewers accepted the BCN-PLGA comparison, no specific evaluation addresses the generalizability caveat.

OpenEval rates claims about MA's chemical properties and future modifications as UNCERTAIN (C157-C159), noting they are plausible inferences lacking direct experimental evidence. No corresponding peer review evaluation addresses these mechanistic hypotheses.

OpenEval supports the authors' acknowledgment of limitations regarding route-dependent AM localization (C163-C165), praising honest assessment of data boundaries. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses these limitation statements.

Peer reviewers support the characterization of the gap in lipid antigen vaccines (C2-C3, C20, C127), with one noting 'few examples of the performance of subunit vaccines integrating lipid antigens.' No corresponding OpenEval result specifically addresses this literature gap characterization.
